2026年上海外滩旅游指南：最佳景点、步行路线、夜景及旅行贴士 
计划第一次去上海外滩游览？
这份完整的《上海外滩指南》涵盖了您在游览前需要了解的一切，包括 1.5 公里的外滩滨水区、著名历史建筑、最佳步行路线、黄浦江游船、南京东路站、附近的景点（如豫园、上海中心大厦和东方明珠电视塔），以及最佳游览时间、摄影技巧和实用旅行建议，帮助您探索上海最具标志性的地标之一。 
 外滩必看亮点 
 历史建筑、和平饭店、海关大楼、外滩公牛和黄浦公园 
 最佳步行体验 
 1.5公里外滩、南京东路、外白渡桥及夜景 
 天际线和河流景色 
 上海中心大厦、东方明珠、黄浦江游船和现代摩天大楼 
 完美的 
 首次来上海的游客、摄影爱好者、家庭游客及私人上海旅游 
外滩概览 
 信息速览信息
 地点上海市中心中山东一路
 长度1.5公里长的海滨长廊
 最佳访问时间清晨、日落前或夜幕降临后
 建议参观时间2–4 小时
 最近的地铁南京东路站，地铁2号线和10号线
 入学咨询免费
 水上巡航30 分钟至 3.5 小时
 附近景点豫园、南京路、上海中心大厦和东方明珠电视塔
外滩值得一游吗？ 
当然。如果您是第一次来上海，外滩绝对应该列入您的行程清单之首。
外滩沿黄浦江绵延1.5公里，是上海最著名的滨水区，也是中国最具代表性的地标之一。它巧妙地融合了昔日公共租界52余座历史建筑与江对岸上海中心大厦、东方明珠电视塔及其他现代摩天大楼的未来主义天际线，形成鲜明对比。
无论您是对历史、建筑、摄影、当地文化感兴趣，还是仅仅想欣赏世界一流的城市天际线，外滩都能为您带来难忘的体验——而且完全免费参观。 
为什么要去外滩？ 
沿着上海标志性的1.5公里滨水长廊漫步。
欣赏哥特式、巴洛克式、装饰艺术式和新古典主义风格的历史建筑。
隔着黄浦江，饱览浦东现代化天际线的全景。
参观和平饭店、海关大楼、外滩牛、黄浦公园等著名地标。
乘坐黄浦江游船，从不同的角度欣赏这座城市。
探索附近的景点，包括豫园、南京路、上海中心大厦和东方明珠电视塔。
在黄浦公园观看当地居民练习太极拳和晨练。
体验上海最壮观的日落和夜景之一。 
外滩必游景点 
漫步上海外滩，就像探索一座露天建筑博物馆。短短1.5公里的路程，您将途经宏伟的殖民时期地标建筑、著名酒店、历史悠久的金融大厦、宁静的江畔公园，以及一些俯瞰浦东现代天际线的最佳观景点。 
和平饭店 
和平饭店是外滩最知名的地标之一。这座装饰艺术风格的杰作于1929年开业，以其绿色的铜屋顶、优雅的外立面以及与老上海的悠久渊源而闻名。
即使您不住在这里，也值得从外面看看或者进去欣赏一下大堂。
亮点：装饰艺术风格建筑、历史悠久的豪华酒店、绿色金字塔屋顶、外滩景观。 
海关 
海关大楼毗邻和平饭店，是外滩的另一标志性建筑。它于1927年竣工，其钟楼近百年来一直俯瞰着黄浦江。
钟楼仍然是中山东路沿线最具标志性的建筑之一。
亮点：标志性钟楼、新古典主义建筑、热门拍照地点。 
前汇丰银行大厦 
香港上海汇丰银行大厦曾是远东地区最令人印象深刻的银行大楼之一。其宏伟的穹顶、古典的柱式以及金融历史反映了上海在20世纪初作为主要银行中心的地位。
亮点：历史悠久的金融地标、古典建筑、上海银行业历史。 
德意志银行 
外滩铜牛象征着上海的金融信心，常被拿来与纽约华尔街铜牛相提并论。它是外滩沿岸一个热门的拍照打卡点，虽然停留时间不长。
亮点：金融象征、旅游拍照点、海滨长廊上的便捷休憩站。 
黄浦公园 
外滩北端的黄浦公园是远离喧嚣的静谧之所。清晨，您经常可以看到当地居民练习太极拳、跳舞、慢跑或进行晨练。
亮点：当地文化、晨练太极、河景、休闲绿地。 
外白渡桥 
外白渡桥，又称花园桥，连接外滩和苏州河，是上海最著名的历史桥梁之一，也是摄影爱好者的热门地点。
从这里，您可以同时欣赏到外滩的历史建筑、苏州河和浦东的现代天际线。
亮点：历史悠久的钢桥、天际线景观、日落摄影。 
外滩最佳步行路线 
游览上海外滩的最佳方式是步行。主要步行街长约1.5公里，您可以悠闲地漫步其中。
这条路线可以在 2 到 3 小时内完成，包括拍照和短暂休息的时间。 
 Stop 停止推荐时间
 南京东路站10分钟
 和平饭店10-15 分钟
 海关大楼及原汇丰银行大楼15-20 分钟
 外滩海滨长廊20-30 分钟
 德意志银行5-10 分钟
 黄浦公园20分钟
 外白渡桥20-30 分钟
建议路线 
从上海地铁2号线或10号线南京东路站出发。沿着上海最繁忙的街道之一南京路向东走，直到到达外滩。
从那里继续沿着滨海大道前行，途经和平饭店、海关大楼、原汇丰银行大厦和外滩牛。然后步行前往黄浦公园，最后到达外白渡桥，欣赏苏州河和浦东天际线的经典景色。 
当地小费 
请在日落前60-90分钟开始您的步行之旅。您将有机会欣赏白日里的外滩，感受黄浦江上绚丽的日落景色，并留下来欣赏上海著名的夜景。 
外滩最佳拍照地点 
无论你使用智能手机还是专业相机，外滩都是上海最佳的摄影地点之一。 
外滩海滨长廊 
这里是拍摄上海天际线、黄浦江、东方明珠电视塔和上海中心大厦的经典地点。
最适合拍摄：城市天际线、日落、夜景、广角照片。 
外白渡桥 
外白渡桥是捕捉老上海与现代浦东风情的绝佳取景地，尤其在日落和夜幕降临时分，景色更是美不胜收。
最适合：桥梁摄影、苏州河摄影、长时间曝光夜景摄影。 
黄浦公园 
清晨来访，可以看到当地人的生活景象，包括太极拳、慢跑和在河边晨练。
最适合：体验当地文化、欣赏晨光、拍摄安静的照片。 
和平酒店外 
费尔蒙和平酒店是建筑摄影的最佳地点之一，尤其是在早上人比较少的时候。
最适合：装饰艺术细节、历史建筑、街头摄影。 
德意志银行 
外滩牛是一处简单却很受欢迎的地标性拍照景点，尤其是在浦东天际线的映衬下，更是如此。
最适合：旅行人像和地标照片。 
摄影技巧 
清晨前往，人会少一些。
为了获得最佳光线，请在日落前到达。
天黑后留下来，可以拍摄灯光璀璨的城市天际线照片。
使用广角镜头拍摄城市天际线。
高峰时段请勿用三脚架阻挡海滨长廊。 
游览外滩的最佳时间 
外滩全天开放，但游览体验会因时间不同而有所变化。 
清晨
清晨最适合悠闲漫步，感受当地文化，而且人也比较少。您或许会在黄浦公园看到当地居民练习太极拳或进行晨练。
下午
下午是欣赏外滩历史建筑的好时机，包括和平饭店、海关大楼和原汇丰银行大厦。夏季，外滩天气炎热潮湿。
日落之前
这是最佳游览时间。建议在日落前一小时左右到达，这样可以欣赏到白天的景色、日落的色彩以及夜晚的灯光秀。
夜晚
夜幕降临，外滩摇身一变，成为上海最壮观的景点之一。历史建筑灯火辉煌，而江对岸的上海中心大厦、东方明珠电视塔和现代摩天大楼则构成了一幅令人叹为观止的天际线。 
最佳季节 
 季节天气推荐
 春季12–22°C步行舒适
 Summer27–34°C天气炎热潮湿，晚上最舒服
 秋季18–26°C天空晴朗，天气宜人。
 冬季2–12°C人少景美
总体而言，春季和秋季是最舒适的季节，但一年四季都值得在晚上来此游览。 
黄浦江游船之旅：值得吗？ 
黄浦江游船是体验外滩和上海天际线的最佳方式之一。沿着江边漫步可以近距离欣赏历史建筑，而乘船游览则可以从水上欣赏黄浦江两岸的景色。 
您会看到什么？ 
游轮航行期间，您可以看到：
外滩历史悠久的滨水区
上海塔
东方明珠电视塔
上海环球金融中心
金茂大厦
陆家嘴金融区
黄浦江夜景 
巡航时间 
 邮轮类型修读年限最适合
 短途观光游轮30-50 分钟初次来访者
 标准游轮60-90 分钟家庭和情侣
 晚餐巡航2–3.5 小时晚间用餐及美景
对于大多数旅行者来说，45 到 60 分钟的观光游船就足够了。 
最佳邮轮旅行时间 
夜间游船最受欢迎，因为可以欣赏到灯火辉煌的外滩和浦东天际线。如果您想要更安静的体验，可以选择白天的游船。 
这值得么？ 
是的，尤其对于初次来上海的游客来说。乘船游览上海能让你更全面地欣赏这座城市的风光，而且在漫步外滩之后，乘船游览更是锦上添花。 
同一天可以游览的附近景点 
外滩的一大优势在于其优越的地理位置。上海众多著名景点都近在咫尺。 
南京路 
南京路是上海最著名的购物街，与外滩自然相连。许多游客从南京东路站步行前往外滩。
行程时间：步行约10分钟。 
豫园 
豫园是上海最著名的古典园林之一，园内亭台楼阁、假山石林、池塘碧波荡漾，建筑风格古朴典雅。周边老城区也是品尝小吃、购买纪念品的热门去处。
行程时间：乘坐出租车或地铁约10分钟。 
上海塔 
上海中心大厦高632米，是中国最高的建筑。其观景台可俯瞰外滩、黄浦江和上海市中心全景。
行程时间：乘坐地铁约需 10-15 分钟。 
东方明珠电视塔 
东方明珠电视塔是上海最知名的地标之一，它隔江与外滩遥遥相望。
很容易将它与外滩游览结合起来，特别是如果您乘坐渡轮、地铁或外滩观光隧道前往浦东的话。 
外滩观光隧道 
外滩观光隧道连接外滩和浦东，位于黄浦江下。它更像是一种旅游体验而非实用的交通方式，但或许能给家庭游客带来乐趣。 
跨河渡轮 
乘坐公共渡轮是横渡黄浦江最便宜、最具当地特色的方式之一。只需支付少量费用，就能欣赏到壮丽的城市天际线。 
半日游和全日游行程示例 
半日外滩行程 
 时间租赁计划
 3:30左右返回码头抵达南京东路站
 4:00左右返回码头步行前往外滩
 4:30左右返回码头参观和平饭店、海关大楼和外滩公牛。
 5:30左右返回码头步行即可到达黄埔公园和外白渡桥
 6:30左右返回码头欣赏日落和夜景
 7:30左右返回码头在外滩附近享用晚餐或在屋顶酒吧小酌一杯。
上海一日游行程 
 时间租赁计划
 中午 9:00 点游览豫园和古城
 中午 11:30 点在豫园或南京路附近吃午饭
 1:00左右返回码头探索南京路
 3:30左右返回码头步行前往外滩
 5:00左右返回码头游览黄浦公园和外白渡桥
 6:30左右返回码头欣赏外滩夜景
 8:00左右返回码头乘坐黄浦江游船
外滩的历史与建筑 
外滩的历史始于19世纪中叶，当时上海在第一次鸦片战争后对外开放。英国租界沿着黄浦江西岸发展起来，该地区逐渐成为上海的商业和金融中心。
20世纪初，各大银行、贸易公司、航运公司和外国机构纷纷在今天的中山东路沿线设立总部。由于其在国际金融和对外贸易中的重要性，该地区被称为“东方华尔街”。
如今，外滩常被誉为一座活生生的建筑博物馆。这里历史建筑林立，风格多样，包括哥特式、巴洛克式、新古典主义、文艺复兴复兴式和装饰艺术风格。和平饭店、海关大楼和汇丰银行大厦等地标性建筑，无不体现着老上海的财富与雄心。
如今外滩之所以如此引人注目，在于它与江对岸的鲜明对比。一边是上海殖民时代的建筑，另一边则是浦东的现代摩天大楼，包括上海中心大厦和东方明珠电视塔。在中国，很少有地方能像这片滨江地区一样，如此清晰地展现出国家的变迁。 
如何前往外滩 
外滩是上海市中心最容易到达的景点之一。 
乘地铁
乘坐上海地铁2号线或10号线到南京东路站。从该站步行约10分钟即可到达外滩。
乘坐出租车或滴滴
目的地可以选择外滩或中山东一路。出租车和滴滴出行都很方便，但周末、节假日和晚间交通可能会比较拥堵。
坐巴士
33路、55路、65路和135路公交车在外滩附近设有站点。
渡轮
您可以乘坐公共渡轮横渡黄浦江，往返于外滩和浦东之间。价格便宜，充满当地风情，而且风景优美。 
 交通信息
 地铁地铁2号线和10号线至南京东路站
 步行距离车站约10分钟路程
 出租车/滴滴交通拥堵时虽然方便但速度较慢。
 公共汽车33号、55号、65号和135号公路
 轮渡过黄浦江到浦东
外滩附近有哪些餐厅？ 
外滩周边地区应有尽有，从上海当地小吃到可以欣赏城市天际线的屋顶餐厅，一应俱全。 
小笼包 
想体验地道美食，不妨尝尝上海著名的汤包——小笼包。豫园、南京路附近以及周边餐馆都能找到不错的选择。 
屋顶餐厅和酒吧 
想要欣赏城市天际线美景，可以选择外滩附近的屋顶餐厅或酒吧。“The Fellas”餐厅是欣赏黄浦江夜景、品尝饮品和享用晚餐的热门之选。 
外滩3号、5号和6号 
外滩三号、五号和六号等历史建筑如今已改建为餐厅、咖啡馆和酒吧。如果您想在用餐的同时感受建筑氛围，这些都是不错的选择。
最佳建议：为了欣赏最佳日落景色，请在日落前 30-60 分钟预订餐桌。 
实用旅行小贴士 
如果想同时欣赏白天和夜晚的景色，请在日落前前往。
清晨前往，人少，还能欣赏当地的太极拳表演。
高峰时段请乘坐地铁，因为交通可能会比较拥堵。
请穿着舒适的鞋子漫步外滩及周边街道。
天黑后留下来欣赏城市天际线的灯光。
将外滩与豫园、南京路、上海中心大厦或东方明珠电视塔结合起来游览。
如果你不喜欢人多的地方，就避开中国的主要节假日。
查看天气预报，尤其是在夏季，上海天气炎热潮湿。
请携带电量充足的相机或手机，以便拍摄夜间照片。
如果想以低廉的价格欣赏过河景色，可以试试乘坐公共渡轮。 
使用 GoChinaQuest 规划您的上海之旅 
外滩不仅仅是上海最著名的滨水区，它更是老上海、现代摩天大楼、江景、当地生活和国际历史交汇融合的令人难忘之地。
如果您想在知识渊博的当地导游的带领下探索外滩、豫园、上海中心大厦、南京路以及上海的隐秘街区，GoChinaQuest 可以帮助您打造符合您节奏和兴趣的私人上海之旅。
乘坐私人导游带领的舒适交通工具，并根据您的旅行需求量身定制灵活的行程。
联系GoChinaQuest，开始规划您的专属上海之旅。 
常見問題解答 
 外滩可以免费参观吗？ 
是的。沿着外滩漫步完全免费。但黄浦江游船、观景台、餐厅和外滩观光隧道等自选项目需要单独购票。 
 什么时候是游览外滩的最佳时间？ 
最佳时间是日落前一小时左右。这样您既能欣赏到白天的景色，又能欣赏到黄浦江上的日落美景，还能看到上海灯火通明后壮丽的天际线。 
 离外滩最近的地铁站是哪个？ 
距离外滩最近的车站是上海地铁2号线和10号线的南京东路站。从那里步行大约10分钟即可到达外滩。 
 我在外滩应该待多久？ 
大多数游客会花 2 到 4 个小时游览海滨，拍摄城市天际线，参观历史建筑，并享受附近的景点。 
 黄浦江游轮之旅值得吗？ 
是的。黄浦江游船之旅能让您从完全不同的视角欣赏上海，既能饱览历史悠久的外滩风光，又能从江面上欣赏浦东的现代天际线。 
 外滩附近有哪些景点可以游览？ 
附近的热门景点包括南京路、豫园、上海中心大厦、东方明珠电视塔、黄浦公园和外滩观光隧道。许多游客会选择一天内游览其中几个景点。

title: 上海南京东路和外滩：热门景点与购物指南
text:
上海南京东路和外滩：热门景点与购物指南
Nightlife
探索上海充满活力的南京东路步行街，这里融合了历史魅力、现代购物和餐饮。步行即可到达外滩，体验上海的都市生活。探索上海南京东路引言
南京东路是上海最充满活力的步行街之一，融合了历史魅力与现代购物和餐饮。全天开放，免费进入，是游客体验上海都市生活和前往外滩等附近地标的理想起点。1. 概览
南京东路（常称东南京路）横贯上海市中心。它曾是一条传统的商业大道，如今已成为一条热闹的步行长廊，两旁林立着百货公司、精品店、咖啡馆以及夜晚亮起的霓虹灯。其中心位置使其成为白天购物和夜晚散步的热门地点。2. 如何前往
乘坐上海地铁即可轻松抵达该区域。乘坐2号线或10号线至南京东路站，然后跟随指示牌。出站后，步行约10分钟即可到达主要的步行区。该站直接连接人民广场和陆家嘴等主要枢纽。3. 景点与活动
– 购物：从大型商场到特色精品店，南京东路提供广泛的零售选择。寻找本地设计师和知名中国品牌以及国际品牌。 – 餐饮：街头小吃摊和国际餐厅在此共存。在信誉良好的店铺品尝小笼包等上海点心。 – 观光：步行街非常适合观察当地人和游客的互动，街头艺人和季节性活动常常增添气氛。 – 摄影：该区域的历史招牌和现代玻璃幕墙形成了鲜明的对比，尤其是在日落时分，非常适合拍照。4. 最佳游览时间
白天是购物和参观附近博物馆的理想时间，而夜晚则在店面和LED显示屏照亮街道时显得格外迷人。工作日通常比周末人少。如果您喜欢更宁静的体验，请在商店开始营业的清晨前来。5. 实用贴士
– 时间与费用：街道全天开放，免费进入。individual shops and restaurants have their own hours。 – 无障碍：大多数人行道宽敞且无障碍；在主要交叉路口寻找坡道。 – 安全：该区域安全且巡逻良好。在繁忙区域注意保管好您的财物。 – 语言：主要酒店和国际商店会讲英语，但建议携带地图或使用翻译应用程序与小店沟通。6. 附近景点
– 外滩：一个风景优美的河滨长廊，拥有殖民时期建筑，距离南京东路仅几步之遥。 – 人民广场：拥有博物馆和文化场馆，可通过相同的地铁线路抵达。 – 上海中心大厦和陆家嘴：乘坐地铁短途即可到达，欣赏天际线景观和现代景点。结论
南京东路轻松融合了购物、餐饮和都市氛围，并享有便捷的地铁交通。全天候开放且免费探索，对于希望感受上海活力的首次访客和回头客来说，这里是必游之地。实用摘要
交通：地铁2号线或10号线至南京东路站；步行约10分钟。 开放时间：全天开放，无门票。https://chinawondersguide.com/zh-Hans/the-bund-shanghai-nanjing-east-road/

title: Shanghai Yu Garden: Tips for What to See & How to Visit
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
Shanghai Yu Garden: Tips for What to See & How to Visit
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Sep. 10, 2026 
Yu Garden, also known as Yuyuan (豫园), is worth visiting on your first Shanghai trip, especially if Suzhou (known for classic Jiangnan gardens) is not on your itinerary. As a first-timer, you should allow 1–2 hours for the garden.
The biggest misunderstanding is that many travelers mix up Yu Garden with the Yuyuan Bazaar outside it.
Inside the garden, you will get a compact introduction to classical Chinese garden design: rockeries, ponds, moon gates, pavilions, and views that change as you walk.
Outside, the Yuyuan Bazaar is a very different experience: busy, commercial, photogenic, and convenient for Shanghai snacks. Add another 1–2 hours if you want to eat and explore the surrounding bazaar.
Yu Garden vs. Yuyuan Bazaar: What Exactly Are You Visiting?
- Yu Garden
- Yuyuan Bazaar
When Is the Best Time to Visit Yu Garden?
Can I Visit Yu Garden at Night?
Yu Garden FAQs
Yu Garden vs. Yuyuan Bazaar: What Exactly Are You Visiting?
Inside Yu Garden: Focus on Rockeries, Water, and Framed Views
The garden is the historic core, and it rewards slow observation.
Don't treat it as a checklist of buildings. The main attraction is how the landscape changes as you move through it.
The Grand Rockery in Yu Garden
Grand Rockery and Water
The Grand Rockery (大假山) is one of the garden's defining features. 
Instead of viewing it from one fixed point, walk around it and look at how the rocks, trees, walls, and water interact. The garden's ponds and water features make the rockery feel larger and more layered than the compact site actually is.
Moon Gates frame the scenery of Yu Garden
Moon Gates and Changing Views
Look through the round moon gates and lattice windows rather than simply walking past them.
A doorway may frame a pavilion.
A wall may hide a pond until you turn the corner.
A narrow passage may suddenly open into a courtyard.
This "view within a view" is one of the best reasons to visit with a guide. 
Our guide will explain with stories why certain openings, rocks, roof decorations, and sightlines were designed the way they were, instead of leaving you to photograph them without context.
Dragon Walls in Yu Garden
Dragon Walls and Traditional Details
Look up as you walk.
The curved dragon walls are among the garden's most recognizable details, with dragon figures running along the tiled walls and rooflines.
These details are easy to miss when the paths are crowded, which is another reason to visit early.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
Explore Yuyuan Bazaar: Food, Photos, and Atmosphere
Step outside the garden walls and you're in a very different space. 
The Yuyuan Bazaar is a modern commercial area built in traditional Chinese architectural style. Its curved roofs, upturned eaves, red-and-gold facades, shops, and lanterns create the "Old Shanghai" look seen in many travel photos.
It is visually convincing, but don't mistake the buildings for the historic garden itself.
Go Here for Shanghai Snacks and "Old Shanghai" Vibe
The area is convenient for trying popular Shanghai foods such as:
- Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant: xiaolongbao (soup dumplings)
- Da Hu Chun: shengjian (pan-fried buns)
- Lu Bo Lang: crab roe pastries
- Tanghulu (candied hawthorn berries)
Spots like Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant are one of the area's best-known names, but don't automatically spend your limited sightseeing time waiting in a long queue simply because a restaurant is famous.
If your priority is food rather than the restaurant name, use the bazaar as a chance to sample one or two local snacks and keep moving.
Shanghai Yu Garden and City God Temple Lantern Festival
Go Here for Evening Photos
The bazaar is particularly photogenic after dark, when lanterns and illuminated facades create the traditional-style Shanghai scene many visitors expect from the area.
That makes the combination especially efficient: Garden in the afternoon → bazaar later → evening meal or Bund at night.
Tip: Add Shanghai City God Temple If You Have 15–30 Minutes
Just outside the south gate of Yu Garden, Shanghai City God Temple (上海城隍庙) is a small Taoist temple dedicated to the city's protective deities.
Entry is free, and the temple is generally open from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM.
If you are interested in Chinese folk religion or Taoist traditions, step inside and take a look at the incense offerings and religious atmosphere.
If not, don't make a special trip just for the temple. Its traditional architecture is easy to appreciate from outside, and your limited time is better spent inside Yu Garden or exploring the surrounding bazaar.
Best use of your time: Treat it as a 15–30-minute add-on while exploring Yuyuan, not as a separate Shanghai attraction.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
When Is the Best Time to Visit Yu Garden?
For the Garden: 9:00–10:00 AM
Yuyuan Garden in the morning
The garden's current regular opening hours are 9:00 AM–4:30 PM, with last entry at 4:00 PM. It is normally closed on Mondays except on statutory holidays.
If the garden itself is your priority, aim close to 9:00 AM.
This matters most on weekends and public holidays, when tour groups and domestic travelers fill the narrow paths by mid-morning. 
Arriving early gives you two advantages: softer light for photos and enough space to stop, look, and appreciate the garden's details without being pushed along by the crowd.
For the Bazaar: Late Afternoon to Evening
Shanghai's Yuyuan Garden Bazaar light up after nightfall.
The bazaar is at its best in the evening, around 7 PM, when the lights come on across the traditional buildings, lanterns glow along the streets, and the area becomes lively with shops, food stalls, and visitors.
On most days, the bazaar is free to enter, so you do not need to buy a Yu Garden ticket just to enjoy the illuminated "Old Shanghai" atmosphere.
There is one important exception: from January to March, the annual Lantern Festival is held around the Jiuqu Bridge and Huxinting (the central area of the bazaar). During the festival, this area requires a separate entrance ticket, so the usual free-entry arrangement does not apply.
For the exact Lantern Festival dates, ticket information, and any other special events taking place during your visit, check the WeChat mini-program "上海豫园" before you go.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
Can I Visit Yu Garden at Night?
Night tour tickets: ¥150 per person for a Chinese-guided tour; ¥190 per person for an English-guided tour
Night-tour hours:
- May–October: 6:30 PM–9:50 PM, Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday
- January–April & November–December: 6:00 PM–9:20 PM, Friday, Saturday and Sunday
Yes, but for a first visit, we recommend seeing the garden by day and saving the evening for the Yuyuan Bazaar.
The night tour is a separate, paid guided experience available only on specific dates. You follow a fixed route through the garden and watch a light-and-shadow show, with the visit lasting about 45 minutes.
That format is the main reason we don't recommend it for most first-time visitors.
You cannot explore the garden at your own pace. If you want to stop at a moon gate, photograph the rockeries from different angles, or linger beside a pond, the fixed route leaves you much less freedom than a daytime visit.

title: How to Plan a Trip to Shanghai Without Rushing Between Spots
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
How to Plan a Trip to Shanghai Without Rushing Between Spots
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Jul. 20, 2026 
For most first-timers, Shanghai is often the first or last stop on a China trip. However, many still aren't sure how to actually "use" the city in their itinerary.
If you only have two or three days in Shanghai, it's tempting to squeeze every famous attraction into your itinerary. That's also why many first-time visitors leave feeling they spent more time crossing the city than enjoying it.
The easiest way to explore Shanghai is to plan each day around one part of the city instead of a checklist of sights.
You'll still see Shanghai's highlights, but you'll also have time to enjoy the cafés, local food, riverside walks, and neighborhoods that make the city memorable.
Why You Should Plan by Neighborhood
How Many Days Do You Really Need?
How to Spend Each Day
Best Areas to Stay in Shanghai
The Best Time to Visit
FAQs
Why You Should Plan by Neighborhood, Not Attractions
To truly experience Shanghai, walking is an unavoidable part of the experience.
Remember one thing before planning your days in Shanghai: the quality of your trip will depend less on how many places you visit, and more on how little you move between different parts of the city.
Shanghai is vast, and its highlights are scattered across districts. Most first-timers try to squeeze the Bund, the Former French Concession, and Shanghai Tower, which are from three distinct districts, into a single day, which makes chasing must-see sights feel exhausting.
Try planning your days by neighborhood. To truly feel the city, it's better to dedicate a half-day or full day to only one district, exploring its sights and its unexpected corners all in one go.
For example, combining the Bund, Nanjing Road, and Yu Garden in the same day gives you a walkable itinerary in Huangpu District, with a flexible pace and deeper experience.
This approach respects the city's scale and rewards you with surprises that no guidebook mentions—hidden courtyards, laid-back locals, and quaint little stalls that you would never spot from a taxi window.
Your days in Shanghai should not just be about sightseeing. They should be about truly experiencing the city, one neighbourhood at a time.
8-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai Tour China Golden Triangle
How Many Days Do You Really Need?
Shanghai is a city that rewards time, but it is also remarkably accommodating to shorter stays. Not all attractions are created equal, and knowing the real time commitment helps you plan realistically.
A 3-day stay is our most recommended; it balances visiting major attractions with a leisurely sightseeing pace. However, the right length depends entirely on your travel style and what you hope to take away from the trip.
2 Days: Focus On the Classic Core
If you really don't have time to see the Bund at night, then taking a walk during the day is also a great option.
Two days are okay for a quick stopover, a brief first warm-up on a trip to China, or a relaxed final stop.
With this timeframe, you should focus exclusively on the classic core: the Bund, Nanjing Road, the Yu Garden, and the Pudong skyline. This is a highlight reel, not a deep dive, which is perfectly fine for a first taste.
You can easily cover all these Shanghai's greatest hits without feeling rushed, if only you stay disciplined and resist the urge to add "just one more" attraction.
3 Days: The Sweet Spot for First-Timers
Three days is the most commonly recommended length for first-time visitors, giving you enough room to see the major landmarks without rushing, while also allowing for one slower day.
The classic three-day structure looks like this: two days for the core sights (the Bund, Nanjing Road, Yu Garden, and Pudong Skyline), and one full day dedicated to the Former French Concession.
This third day is where the magic happens.
No need to be rushed to ticket booths or squeeze yourself into the observation decks; just enjoy a walk along leafy streets, hopping café stops, and the kind of unhurried wandering that makes a city feel like your own.
If you appreciate the charm of classic Chinese water towns, you might consider skipping the strolls through the Former French Concession and instead visiting Zhujiajiao or Tongli water towns to admire the classical aesthetics of Jiangnan.
4－5 Days: Explore the Complete Shanghai, or Its Nearby Cities
Experience traditional Chinese water town by taking a boat tour in Zhujiajiao.
For most travelers, four to five days is the ideal length to plan a trip with a higher tolerance for emergencies.
You can tick off the classics, spend a full day in the Former French Concession, or add a detour, whether that is Disneyland, a day trip to a water town like Zhujiajiao, or simply revisiting a neighborhood you liked, and still have a buffer day.
Don't underestimate the extra day that gives you weather flexibility and room to rest. Shanghai is a walking city, and fatigue is real.
With four or five days, you never have to choose between seeing something and catching your breath. You can do both.
Still deciding how long to spend in Shanghai? We can help you balance Shanghai with destinations like Suzhou, Hangzhou, or Beijing based on your interests instead of following a fixed route.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
How to Spend Each Day Without Crossing the City
Shanghai's attractions are clustered into distinct neighborhoods.
For a smooth and leisurely pace, try your best to dedicate each day to only one area and explore it thoroughly, letting the neighborhood itself become the experience rather than a collection of disconnected stops.
Day 1: The Bund & Huangpu Core
Begin your day at the historic heart of Shanghai, the Bund, arrive before 8:30 AM if you want to see locals exercising and photograph the skyline without tour groups.
You can enjoy a quiet walk along the riverbank, taking in the colonial-era architecture on one side and the futuristic Pudong skyline on the other. By around 9:30 AM, group tours begin arriving, and the promenade becomes noticeably busier.
From there, walk west into Nanjing Road, one of Shanghai's most famous shopping streets.
Unless shopping is one of your priorities, treat Nanjing Road as the easiest walking route between the Bund and Yu Garden rather than a destination on its own.
In the afternoon, head to Yu Garden and the surrounding City God Temple bazaar. This is Shanghai's remaining side of traditional China, with classical pavilions, winding bridges, and lively street food stalls.
End your day back at the Bund for the spectacular nightly view, when the entire skyline illuminates across the river.
Why this works: This route covers Shanghai's most iconic highlights, with everything reached within walking distance. No taxis, no metro transfers, just a comfortable day of strolling through Shanghai's postcard-like corridors.
Day 2: The French Concession & Jing'an District
Dedicate your second day to Shanghai's most walkable neighborhood.
Start at Wukang Road and the iconic Wukang Building, then wander through the leafy streets of the former French Concession. This area is packed with historic villas, boutique shops, and street-side cafés that feel a world away from the skyscrapers.
Turn north to explore Anfu Road for vintage stores, stop for coffee at a garden café, or a street-front restaurant for lunch.
If time allows, you can visit the nearby Jing'an Temple or Jade

text:
Home
 Travel Guide
How to Plan a Trip to Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai
Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai are China's most popular three destinations and are known as the "China's golden triangle". These top three cities offer a diverse and fascinating outlook on China's ancient history, modern development, and unique cultural experiences. This article will help you plan a perfect trip to these cities.
Content Preview
How Many Days to Spend
A Classic Itinerary
How to Travel
Which City to Start
Travel Cost
Hotels Suggestions
Best Time to Visit
Hong Many Days to Spend in Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai
The amount of time you should spend in Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai depends on the pace of your trip and your preferences. However, we recommend you spend at least 7–8 days to deeply experience these cities' cultures and attractions. If you have around 9–10 days for your trip to China, you would ideally spend 3 days in each of these three cities.
However, if you have less time, you may need to prioritize which activities and landmarks you want to see or consider just visiting one or two cities in more depth.
A Classic 8-Day Beijing, Xi'an, Shanghai Itinerary
With 8 days in these cities, you can cover most of the highlights and experience some cultural activities to enrich your knowledge about China.
Days 1–4: Beijing (Visit the Great Wall and Forbidden City)
In Beijing, spending two days for city sightseeing is recommended, including the Forbidden City, Summer Palace, and Temple of Heaven. To help you get a better understanding of the largest and best-preserved ancient imperial palace, our private guide would help you explore 12 carefully-selected places in the Forbidden City, which is definitely an improvement on the standard group tours that are herded down the crowded central axis.
Spend a day to explore country's top landmark: the Great Wall of China. For travelers with kids or seniors, we suggest you visit a less-crowded and easy-walking section called Mutianyu. If you would prefer a more varied and active exploration, you could hike from the Jinshanling section to the Simatai section, where you could have a romantic picnic dinner on the Great Wall with our special arrangements.
If you are interested in authentic Beijinger life, we can arrange a hutong day tour, when you can visit a local family and take a rickshaw ride, and wander around a hutong community with local markets and parks.
Days 5–6: Xi'an
Xi'an is well-known for its historical relics. Spend a day to explore the different pits holding the Terracotta Army and learn about more about Chinese history. Our guide would show you around the Terracotta Army and unveil some secrets of this world wonder candidate. See the hundreds of life-size warriors at the site, and get to know how ancient craftsmen made them. Visit a traditional cave dwelling and learn how to make clay warriors. You can make a small one with some expert guidance and bring it home as a souvenir.
For the rest of your time in Xi'an, we would arrange a biking tour on Xi'an City Wall and a chance to try local street food and snacks in the Muslim Quarter.
Days 7–8: Shanghai
In Shanghai, join our In-Depth Bund Culture Discovery Tour to explore The Bund, which is a must-visit place in Shanghai. Our guide would lead you to the old parts of the Bund where you would travel back in time to the golden age of the Bund in the 1920s. You would walk a route that tourists seldom find by themselves, see the most authentic architecture, and hear some interesting stories that you'll never find in history books.
For the rest of time in Shanghai, you would be free to do numerous relaxing activities, including experiencing local fashionable activities, appreciating art, exploring folk customs, or just shopping.
China Golden Triangle TourBeijing–Xi'an–Shanghai
How to Travel Between Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai
Being major travel destinations in China, it is convenient to travel between the three cities by high-speed train and plane. For a richer experience and a level of comfort that is better than plane travel, we recommend you take a bullet train from Beijing to Xi'an or Shanghai, which takes about 4½ to 5 hours. It is better to take a flight between Shanghai and Xi'an as it takes about 6–7 hours by train. If you would prefer the quickest transport, flights between any of the three cities take about 2–4 hours. However, you may spend a significant amount of time on the road to/from airports, especially during rush hours.
Which City Should I Visit First?
Both Beijing and Shanghai are major entry/exit cities with abundant international and domestic flights. We recommend you start your trip in Shanghai or Beijing, with Beijing being the preferred starting city for most customers.
Costs for a Trip to Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai
Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai are popular travel destinations, which have a higher service cost than lower-tier and less-popular China cities. For a private tour, the average cost per day is about US$220–350 per person, including flights/trains within China, 4- or 5-star hotels, lunches, attractions, guides, and private transport.
For an 8-day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai tour that would be around US$1,760–2,800 per person. When you book with us, if you cancel up to three weeks before departure, you would receive a 100% refund of any payments made to China Highlights (more details here⇒).
9-Day Beijing ,Xian and Shanghai Tour China Family Classic Tour 
Accommodation Choices in Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai
In Beijing, if you prefer a more central location for entertainment and shopping, then you are recommended to choose a hotel in the Wangfujing area. If you want a traditional Beijing-style accommodation experience, we recommend a hutong-style hotel.
In Xi'an, if you would like to have taste of the traditional atmosphere of Xi'an, we recommend you stay in the Walled City Area near the medieval city walls of Xi'an. If you would like to have easy access to many restaurants and shops, we recommend the area near two iconic landmarks of Xi'an — the Bell Tower and Drum Tower.
In Shanghai, hotels around the Bund and Nanjing Road are popular choices if you prefer a bustling vibe and great night views. If you would prefer relatively quiet surroundings with an old colonial vibe, we recommend the French Concession.

Best Times to Visit Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai
For comfortable weather (warm, sunny, and dry), the best time to visit Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai is autumn, especially in September and October. The rainy season in Beijing, Xi'an, and Shanghai typically occurs in the summer months between June and August, which is characterized by frequent afternoon rains that don't last for long. In case of rainy weather, we would adjust your itinerary to make sure your travel experience is not affected.
The peak seasons are the first weeks of May and October, followed by summer holidays. In these peak times, the price of hotels and airfares can go up by 50 to 100%. If you plan to travel during these periods, please book at least 6 months to 1 year in advance as hotels and train tickets particularly are sold out quickly during these times.

title: Shanghai Weather in March 2027: Cold to Warm, Spring Arrives
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
Shanghai Weather in March 2027: Cold to Warm, Spring Arrives
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Jun. 2, 2026 
March is the beginning of spring in Shanghai, but winter hasn't fully gone yet. Normally, you can expect average temperatures to range from 6-13°C (43-55°F). 
Early March can still feel cold and damp, with occasional light rain. By late March, afternoons become pleasantly mild, often reaching 15-17°C (59-63°F). Sometimes, you may even have the illusion that early summer has arrived early, with the maximum temperature on March 28, 2026, being 23 °C (73°F). 
Rainfall averages 10-12 days per month (13 days in 2026), with about 81 mm (3.2 inches), which is a lot more than in February, but usually light and brief. 
Is March a Good Time to Visit Shanghai?
Cherry blossoms in Shanghai Century Park in spring
Yes, March is a good time to visit Shanghai, especially if you love Chinese classic Jiangnan water town scenery, or spring cherry blossoms, and don't mind a few rainy days. 
Early March is still like winter, with fewer tourists, lower rates, and less color. But compared to February (still cold, Chinese New Year may linger) and April (peak blossom season but also more crowds and higher prices), late March is quieter and more affordable, and offers pleasant afternoons with a lively, blooming atmosphere. 
The biggest draw for locals is cherry blossom season, which typically starts in late March and runs through early April. So avoid weekends and stick to weekdays if you want to enjoy a quieter blooming scenery.
8-Day Zhangjiajie, Furong, Fenghuang, and Shanghai TourShanghai- Zhangjiajie - Furong - Fenghuang- Changsha 
What to See and Do in Shanghai in March
Besides the iconic attractions that can be visited at any time for first-timers to Shanghai, such as the Bund, the French Concession, and the Yu Garden, we'd love to take you to see the beautiful scenery that only comes with this season. 
Visit Classic Jiangnan Water Town: Zhujiajiao or Tongli
Our clients visited Zhujiajiao Water Town at the end of March.
No trip to Shanghai is complete without experiencing a classic Jiangnan water town. 
March's mild weather and soft drizzles make these ancient canal towns even more poetic, giving out classic Chinese ink-like painting scenery with misty days, white-walled houses, arched stone bridges, and willow branches turning green. 
Zhujiajiao Water Town, which is just a 1-hour drive away from downtown, is the most convenient choice for first-timers. Take a boat tour to appreciate the town from the water, stroll along cobblestone streets for local snacks, and walk leisurely in the ancient gardens built hundreds of years ago. 
For a quieter alternative, if you travel on weekends, Tongli Water Town offers fewer tourists and a more authentic exploration. You can try a traditional Chinese cheongsam makeover and take charming photos beside the river, as if you've stepped back in time.
Admire Shanghai Cherry Blossom
Night view of Nanpu Bridge and streets in Shanghai during spring cherry blossom season
Late March (normally after March 25th) is when Shanghai's cherry trees begin to bloom. We've organized a themed route that takes about 2–3 hours at a leisurely pace, with plenty of spots to sit and enjoy. 
However, it's best to visit on a weekday morning for the best light, pleasant weather, and the fewest people.
Start at Hongkou Football Stadium Subway Station, Exit 6. Right outside, you'll step into a cherry blossom square lined with dozens of Somei-yoshino trees. 
From there, walk about 2 minutes to Kaveh Kane, where you can buy a coffee to go or take a quick break. Continue to the Breeze Hall (微风礼堂), a modern glass building framed by flowering trees.
Next, stroll down Tian'ai Road (Sweet Love Road), a short lane lined with cherry trees and heart‑shaped signs that create a romantic atmosphere. This leads directly into Lu Xun Park, where you can take a leisurely stroll surrounded by mature cherry trees.
Finally, end your walking tour at the Falling Cherry Pond (落樱池), a quiet corner where petals drift onto the water, creating a picture-perfect scene. You can enjoy a gentle breeze from the water's surface as you relax.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in March
Due to March being a transition month between winter and spring, we'd like to divide the advice by when you travel to be more specific.
If You Travel During Early-to-Mid March (1st－15th)...
In early March, a light down jacket is fine to wear in Shanghai.
Winter still lingers in this period, so you can expect chilly mornings and cool daily weather, with occasional light rain and wind. 
Pack a thermal base layer (long-sleeved), a sweater or fleece, and a waterproof coat to cope with rain. A scarf, gloves, and a warm hat are necessary if you plan to be outdoors for morning exploration or evening strolls. 
It is a must to wear water-resistant sneakers or boots with thick socks if you decide to embark on a city walk. What's more, bring an umbrella and a small backpack with you to shed layers when you enter a heated indoor space.
If You Travel During Mid-to-Late March (16th－31st)...
At the end of March, both hoodies and windbreakers are suitable.
Typically, spring arrives with warmer days. 
You'll still need layers for morning and evening adventures, but you can leave the heavy gloves at home. Pack long-sleeved shirts, a light sweater or hoodie, and a waterproof windbreaker will be more suitable. 
A scarf is still useful for windy days on the Bund or by the water. Wear comfortable shoes for long-distance walking. Sunglasses and a compact umbrella are essential, since March showers are short but frequent, with a sunny day coming behind.

March gives you one of the best times to visit Shanghai, either exploring quiet water towns or admiring the first pink blossoms, and all the iconic sights, without the April rush.

title: Shanghai Weather in July 2026: Hot, Muggy, Sunny, with Tips
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
Shanghai Weather in July 2026: Hot, Muggy, Sunny, with Tips
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Apr. 15, 2026 
July is one of Shanghai's hottest months, comparable to August. Average temperatures range from 26–31°C (79–88°F), with highs typically peaking around 3 PM (in July 2025, it reached 38°C / 100°F).
The "plum rainy season" ends in July, so rainfall decreases compared to June, averaging 11 rainy days (about 125 mm / 4.9 in). You can expect more sunny days from July 21 to 31, but keep in mind that this period is also likely to be the hottest of the month.
What's more, typhoon activity increases toward the end of the month, so it's wise to check the weather forecast if you're traveling then.
Is It a Good Time to Visit Shanghai in July?
Summer at Guyi Garden, a Jiangnan-style garden in Shanghai
July is one of the worst times to visit Shanghai, but that doesn't mean you can't have a great trip.
It all depends on how you handle the heat, plan your days, and use a few smart strategies.
1. Don't Overschedule Daytime Activities
July days are hot. Plan outdoor sightseeing before 11:00 AM or after 5:00 PM, when temperatures are generally below 28°C (82°F) and much more comfortable.
Between 11:00 AM and 5:00 PM, stay cool indoors: visit the air-conditioned Shanghai Museum, find a nice café for afternoon tea, or head back to your hotel for a nap before exploring a nearby shopping mall.
If you must be outside during peak heat, remember to use sunscreen and drink plenty of water to avoid heatstroke.
2. Plan Your Itinerary for Weekdays
July and August are summer vacation months for Chinese students, so weekends are especially crowded as families go out together.
Weekdays, especially Tuesdays and Wednesdays, are noticeably quieter.
For popular family attractions like Shanghai Disneyland, choose a weekday and consider buying early bird tickets or VIP passes. This can save you hours of queuing (popular rides like Zootopia: Hot Pursuit can have wait times of over 2 hours).
China Golden Triangle TourBeijing–Xi'an–Shanghai
3. Book as Early as Possible
July is peak season, so hotel and transportation rates rise sharply.
Reserve your trip and accommodation at least three months in advance for better prices. For attraction tickets, book at least 7 days ahead since many sell out quickly.
4. Will I Be Affected by the Typhoon?
Shanghai's typhoon season is mainly from July to September, with peak periods in late July and late August.
But it is not a big concern with a well-planned itinerary. Normally, typhoons only affect flights for 1–3 days. So just keep your bookings flexible, and leave some buffer time in your itinerary in case of delays.
Want a stress-free trip? Travel with China Highlights. We offer flexible schedules, door-to-door transportation, and professional guides to help you make the most of your July visit.
12-Day Tour: Beijing – Xi'an – Guilin/Yangshuo – ShanghaiClassic Wonders 
How to Spend A Day in Shanghai in July
Morning (7–11 AM): Enjoy Outdoor Activities
Zhujiajiao Water Town, Shanghai
In July, sunrise is around 5 AM, and sunset is around 7 PM.
To avoid the sweltering heat, schedule outdoor activities as early as possible. You'll enjoy cooler temperatures and quieter attractions before the crowds and heat arrive.
Zhujiajiao Water Town: You could not miss out on "Shanghai's Venice". Stroll along cobblestone streets, admire the quaint houses, sample local delicacies, or take a boat trip through the water town.
French Concession Citywalk: Embark on a citywalk through Shanghai's colonial history, experience the blend of Chinese and Western architectural styles, and grab a ice coffee from a street vendor to refresh yourself.
Yu Garden: This 500-year-old classical Chinese garden not only showcases the fusion of Eastern aesthetics and nature, but also brings a touch of coolness to you in the sweltering summer.
Midday (11 AM–5 PM): Escape the Heat
The 360-degree transparent glass observation deck in Oriental Pearl Tower, Shanghai
The weather becomes quite hot and humid, so air-conditioned indoor attractions are your best bet.
Alternatively, stroll through a shopping mall and have afternoon tea, or return to your hotel after a light lunch to relax in air-conditioned comfort.
Consider taking a dip in the pool and waiting for the temperature to drop before heading out again.
Shanghai Museum (East Campus): As one of China's four top museums, you can admire some of the most precious historical collections, including bronzes, jades, coins, and calligraphy works from thousands of years ago.
Oriental Pearl Tower: What sets the Oriental Pearl Tower apart from other skyscrapers in Shanghai is its 360-degree transparent glass observation deck, a child-friendly VR roller coaster, and a romantic revolving restaurant, perfectly catering to the needs of all kinds of people.
Xintiandi: This is where ancient Shikumen architecture blends with modern shopping malls, and it has a richer historical heritage than other commercial districts. Stroll through this shopping area, and check out any trendy brands or popular restaurants that catch your eye.
Evening and Night (After 5 PM): Explore Vibrant Shanghai
Shanghai night market barbecue street food
As the sun sets, the summer heat fades, and city lights begin to illuminate Shanghai, the famous "city that never sleeps".
It is just waking up, ready for you to explore.
The Bund: Enjoying the beautiful night view of the famous skyline from the Bund is a must-do for all first-time visitors to Shanghai, which can be quite crowded. We suggest you head to the Sinar Mas Plaza on the North Bund to avoid the crowds, grab a chilled drink, and wait for nightfall to light up the skyline.
Sijing Night Market (泗泾夜市): Start your food adventure at Shanghai's most bustling and largest night market. Browse the dazzling array of street food and let the vibrant atmosphere fill your senses.
Huaihai Road: This is Shanghai's most down-to-earth, social, and lively bar street. You can find a bar that interests you and relax with a drink to unwind after a long day.
What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in July
July in Shanghai is hot, humid, and rainy.
Pack lightweight, breathable clothing, like several short-sleeved T-shirts, shorts or light wide-leg pants, and a light sun-protective jacket. Choose comfortable sneakers or sandals, and opt for light-colored, quick-drying fabrics.
Remember to always carry a dual-purpose umbrella (for sun and rain) for shade and to deal with sudden showers. High SPF sunscreen, a sun hat, and sunglasses are also essential.
For extra comfort, bring a small handheld fan and a pack of wet wipes and tissues to help you stay cool.

title: Shanghai Weather in November 2026: Vibrant Autumn Colors
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
Shanghai Weather in November 2026: Vibrant Autumn Colors
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated May. 8, 2026 
November is one of the best months to visit Shanghai. Autumn is at its peak, offering mild, sunny days with little rainfall and noticeably fewer crowds than October.
The city averages only 5 rainy days this month, with total rainfall of about 48 mm (1.9 inches).
Daytime temperatures hover around a pleasant 17°C (62°F), perfect for outdoor exploration and city strolls. Evenings cool down quickly, dropping to around 10°C (50°F), so packing an extra layer is essential to stay comfortable.
Is November a Good Month to Visit Shanghai?
Red maple leaves on the river in Shanghai Gongqing Forest Park
Yes, November is an excellent month to visit Shanghai. 
The weather is crisp, sunny days are plentiful, and after the October Golden Week, China's major holidays are over. You can expect fewer crowds and gradually cooling prices, which is a perfect combination for a relaxed city trip.
However, November is not a single, uniform month. Based on recent weather patterns, we divide it into three distinct periods:
1. Early November (1－10): Warm, Sunny, but "Transitional" Foliage
This is your last chance to enjoy Shanghai's lingering warmth before the first winter chill arrives, which is ideal for travelers who are sensitive to cold or don't prioritize peak foliage.
Temperatures are still mild, ranging from 14－20°C (57－68°F), with plenty of sunshine. The autumn colors are just beginning, so you are more likely to see a mix of green leaves turning yellow. 
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
2. Mid-November (11－20): Cold Snap, Rain, and Rapid Color Change
Around mid-month, a cold front typically sweeps through, bringing 4－5 days of rain and a sharp temperature drop of around 8°C (46°F). 
This sudden chill accelerates the autumn colors, and you may be amazed by leaves turning vibrant red and gold almost overnight. 
However, outdoor activities become cold and damp. If your trip falls during this window, we recommend balancing your itinerary with more indoor attractions like museums, art galleries, or shopping malls to stay comfortable and dry.
3. Late November (21－30): Peak Autumn Scenery with Pleasant Days
By late November, autumn is in full glory. Temperatures stabilize at a cool 7－15°C (45－59°F), and sunny days return. 
The city's famous "no-sweeping" policy leaves fallen golden leaves lining the streets, creating postcard-worthy scenes. 
It's the perfect time to stroll through tree-lined avenues like Wukang Road of the French Concession, coffee in hand, soaking in the serene beauty of Shanghai at its most poetic.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
What to See and Do in Shanghai in November?
As a first-timer to Shanghai, beyond the Bund (admire the dazzling evening skyline) and the Shanghai Tower (the world's third tallest building), November in Shanghai offers a quieter, more poetic treasure: the autumn colors. 
This is the month when the city dresses in gold and red, inviting you to slow down and savor its seasonal beauty.
For Early Autumn Colors: Chinese Traditional Gardens
Early autumn scenery in Yu Garden, Shanghai
Yu Garden (Yuyuan) and Guyi Garden are at their most charming in early November. 
Although the autumn leaves have not yet all changed color, the first blush of red maple leaves and turning ginkgo trees have already added a lot of color to the ancient pavilions and winding corridors.
Unlike the crowded peak season, you can enjoy some serene November mornings here, which is perfect for a leisurely stroll through the Chinese traditional Jiangnan garden aesthetic.
For Golden Sycamore Strolls: The French Concession
Autumn urban road landscape in Wutong District, French Concession, Shanghai
In mid-to-late November, the tree-lined avenues of the French Concession transform into magical tunnels of golden plane tree leaves, especially around Sinan Mansions on Sinan Road. 
Walking on this thick carpet of autumn feels like stepping into a postcard. But beyond the beautiful scenery, our guide will also take you on a journey to learn about the legendary figure, Du Yuesheng. This once-powerful mob boss rose from nothing to become the "Emperor of Shanghai's Underworld."
For Vibrant Ginkgo and Local Life: Gubei Huangjincheng Avenue
For a more locally cherished autumn spot, head to Huangjincheng Avenue (Golden City Avenue) in Shanghai Changning Hongqiao Gubei Community, which is more authentic, lively, and less touristy.
Here, a dazzling avenue of ginkgo trees turns brilliant yellow, creating a canopy of sunshine. You will be welcomed by a neighborhood that buzzes with family-friendly energy, see children kicking through leaves, couples taking photos, and small shops selling warm treats. 
For Seasonal Magic: Shanghai Disneyland
November is a transitional month of pure magic at Shanghai Disneyland. 
You may still see the park decorated with a Halloween theme in Early November. By late November, the park officially launches its Christmas season, complete with giant Christmas trees, snowfall on Mickey Avenue, and festive parades. 
If you're traveling with children, this is an absolute must. The cooler weather also makes waiting in lines far more comfortable than in summer.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in November
November in Shanghai means warm afternoons but chilly evenings, so layering is your best friend.
Pack a few long-sleeved shirts, a fleece or sweater, and a waterproof jacket that can handle drizzles. Jeans or comfortable trousers work fine for most days.
Don't forget a warm scarf when it becomes your best friend when the sun goes down. Comfortable, waterproof walking shoes are a must, especially if the rain appears. Sunglasses can also be useful on bright autumn days.

Shanghai
 Hailed as the “Magical City”, Shanghai is a dynamic metropolis that enchants visitors with its eclectic mix of modern charm and historical glamour. Our English-guided private Shanghai tours curated for 2027 & 2028 invite you to saunter down the iconic Bund, get lost in the colonial-era architecture, and gaze upon the glitzy skyline of Lujiazui, while getting swept up in the mesmerizing neon-lit night views along the Huangpu River. Also, the classic Chinese aesthetics of Yu Garden and the tranquil canals of Zhujiajiao Water Town are sure to leave you spellbound. If time permits, consider extending your Shanghai tour packages to atmospheric Suzhou, Hangzhou, or the majestic peaks of Huangshan.

 FAQs on Shanghai Tours
 Where to go in Shanghai for first-timers?
 For first-timers, the Bund is an absolute must-see, where historic European architecture faces the futuristic skyline anchored by the Oriental Pearl Tower across the Huangpu River. Be sure to catch the dazzling night view when the iconic skyscrapers glow in kaleidoscopic lights, followed by a stroll through the bustling energy of nearby Nanjing Road.
 For a deep dive into history and traditions, it is recommended to explore Shanghai Museum’s vast collections, the classic Yu Garden featuring elegant pavilions and zigzag bridges, the Yuyuan Bazaar and City God Temple area filled with the old town’s buzz, and the Jade Buddha Temple offering a spiritual escape. For a city walk, Xintiandi, Tianzifang, and the Former French Concession offer the best routes to discover artistic alleys brimming with fancy boutiques and cafes tucked inside traditional stone-gate houses. For a slow pace, escape to Zhujiajiao Water Town to immerse yourself in its quaint atmosphere, with a scenic boat ride past whitewashed residences, historic stone bridges, and authentic street food stalls.
 How many days is enough for a Shanghai trip?
 2 to 3 days are enough to cover the sprawling city’s main highlights. Spend one day downtown for the iconic Bund with a Huangpu River cruise. Visit the Yu Garden and Shanghai Museum for history exploration, and stroll around the flashy Xintiandi or artistic Tianzifang neighborhoods. The second day is to linger over the picture-perfect Tongli or Zhujiajiao Water Town, where scenic canals, arch bridges, and hand-rowed boats reveal the ‘old China’ lifestyle. On the third day, take in panoramic views of the megacity from a skyscraper observatory. Spend your afternoon exploring the tech-forward flagship stores of Nanjing Road or sampling local delicacies on Huanghe Road. Alternatively, escape into a full day of magic at Asia’s largest Disney resort.   
1 day: For Shanghai layover tours in one day, focus on the urban core: the Bund, Lujiazui high-rises, Shanghai Museum, and Yu Garden area, or spend half the day in Zhujiajiao Water Town and the other half exploring city landmarks according to your interests.
4-5 days or more: Apart from the quintessential experiences within the city, escape to the nearby classic water towns like Wuzhen and Zhouzhuang, take a day trip to the neighboring cities of Suzhou, Hangzhou, Wuxi, or Nanjing, or extend your private Shanghai tour to farther well-known destinations, such as Beijing, Xi’an, and Zhangjiajie. Welcome to connect with our English-speaking travel consultants to curate your bespoke itinerary.
 Which month is the best to visit Shanghai?
 Generally, the premium time for your Shanghai vacation packages is the spring from March to May and autumn from September to November, when the weather is pleasant with average temperatures between 15-25℃ (60-77 ℉), receiving less rainfall. Cherry blossoms, peach blossoms, and tulips reach full bloom, and paulownia trees begin to be luxuriant in warm spring; and in fall, the gingko trees along the Bund transform into golden colors in pleasantly cool days. Dress in layers, like hoodies with shirts or thin sweaters, especially in cool mornings and nights.
January is the coldest month, with temperatures dropping to around 5℃ (41℉), plus the high humidity, making you feel even colder than it actually is. June and July, when the humidity builds up, bring buckets of rain, and July is the hottest month of the year. Please avoid the busy holidays, such as the May Day break, the National Day holiday from Oct. 1st to 7th, and the Chinese New Year falling in January or February.
 Is Shanghai expensive for tourists?
 While Shanghai is generally more expensive than other mainland Chinese cities like Xi’an, Chengdu, or even the capital Beijing, it remains significantly more affordable than global hubs like Hong Kong, Tokyo, or major European cities. On average, a comfortable Shanghai trip ranges from USD 120 to 180 per person per day.
For instance, a quality 3 or 4-star hotel costs between USD 70-110 per night. While upscale restaurants can exceed USD 70 per person, a mid-range meal typically costs USD 17-30, and a quick meal, like a McDonald's Big Mac set, costs only USD 5-7. A Starbucks coffee is USD 4-6, while the local chains like Luckin Coffee cost just USD 2-3. Public transport is remarkably efficient and cheap. A bus or metro ride starts at just 40 US cents. Taxis are also accessible, with a starting fare of USD 2 for the first 3 km.
 What is the easiest way to get around Shanghai?
 The easiest way to navigate Shanghai is via its world-class metro network. Spanning over 560 miles, it offers a fast and economical way to reach almost any corner of the city. A one-way fare ranges from USD 0.4 to 2 depending on the distance. For a thrill, try the superfast maglev train from Pudong Airport towards downtown, USD 7 one-way, which is not only an efficient transfer but also a unique experience. To cross the Huangpu River, consider the local public ferry instead of traditional bus or metro. For only 30 US cents, you can enjoy a brief but scenic transit that offers a great perspective of the skyline from the water.
Of course, for tourists who are unsure about the local transport, taxi is a hassle-free and quite affordable choice. The taxi service here is highly efficient and significantly cheaper than in Europe or North America. The starting fare is USD 2 for the first 3 km, followed by a rate of USD 0.4 per kilometer. The ride-hailing app Didi boasts greater convenience and costs even less.
 Is Shanghai a walkable city?
 Yes, it certainly is! The city is suitable for walking to slow down and stop to appreciate its historical charm, and immerse yourself in retro-themed boutiques and cafes lining the narrow streets. The Bund is the premier choice, flanked by 52 imposing Western-style buildings on the west and the Huangpu River with towering skyscrapers on the east. Shanghai Transportation
Shanghai, as the most modern international metropolis in China, has an all-round development of transportation system. No matter where you are now – overseas or in other parts of China – there are efficient and convenient transportation modes you can choose to reach Shanghai, and the diverse transportation options within the city also contribute to a worry-free Shanghai journey for you.
How to Get to Shanghai?
1. By Air – the Most Efficient Way to Arrive Shanghai from AfarSuppose your first destination in China is Shanghai, taking the plane is the most efficient way. Shanghai airports rank among the top three busiest airports in the world because of their wide coverage of airline service and dense air routes over the globe. At present, there are two airports in Shanghai – Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, with the former being the major international aviation hub whose air routes are available in more than 130 cities overseas, and the latter mainly providing flight service in Chinese mainland mostly, as well as a few short-haul routes to Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea.
By virtue of its extensive and convenient air service, Shanghai has constantly been the first stop when a large number of international tourists travel in China, as well as the transfer stop as many tourists travel to other Asian countries such as Japan and South Korea. Terminal of Shanghai Pudong International Airport  
2. By Bullet Train – More Efficient Option to Reach Shanghai within a Short-to-Medium Distance
Taking the bullet train can be a good choice if you depart from other Chinese cities to Shanghai, since 97% of Chinese cities have direct high-speed rail connections to Shanghai. In particular, if your departure location is not too far away from Shanghai, taking the high-speed train will be more cost-effective. For instance, it only takes 30 - 60 minutes to arrive Shanghai from its neighboring cities in the Yangtze River Delta including Suzhou, Hangzhou, Nanjing, etc. and 4 - 5 hours from central part of China like Beijing.
Nevertheless, the train journey from farther cities such as Xi'an and Chongqing to Shanghai takes a relatively longer time, approximately 6 hours. Therefore, if you have a tight schedule, you are more recommended to travel by air, which allows you to arrive in 2 - 2.5 hours.
Among all railway stations in the city, Shanghai Railway Station is the closest one to Shanghai downtown, followed by Shanghai South Railway Station and Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station. They all link with metro lines that can reach the Bund in 20 - 40 minutes. Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station Shanghai Bullet Trains

3. By Cruise
Thanks to its advantageous location along the coast, Shanghai also has a well-developed maritime transportation system. The international cruise routes mainly include Japan, South Korea, and some Southeastern Asian countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and finally arrive at Shanghai Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal. Shanghai Cruise Shanghai Cruise on the Sea  
How to Get Around in Shanghai?
The transportation within Shanghai is efficient and travelers-friendly as well, with a diverse range of public transportation modes for you to pick. Subway, buses, and taxis all provide real-time service for you to visit various attractions and commercial districts; feature transportation like ferries, sightseeing buses, and the bund sightseeing tunnel are also available, not only facilitating your itinerary but also offering you unique experience to appreciate beautiful views of Shanghai.
1. By Metro
Taking the metro is preferred for traveling around Shanghai, especially during morning and evening peak hours on weekdays, which helps you in avoiding the traffic congestion on the roads. Besides, taking the subway is very economical, with a one-way fare ranging from CNY 3 to 26.
Currently, there are 20 metro lines in service in Shanghai. They not only connect the two airports and major railway stations, but also cover most attractions and commercial districts. For example, Shanghai Metro Line 1 links Hongqiao International Airport, Hongqiao Railway Station and the Bund; and Line 2 passes through Pudong International Airport, Shanghai Railway Station, Shanghai South Railway Station, People's Square, as well as Shanghai Tower, etc. Train Platform of Shanghai Metro Line 2 Inside Shanghai Metro Train

Shanghai Metro Maps
How to Take Shanghai Metro 
2. By Taxi Shanghai Taxi If you are burdened with luggage, then taking the taxi would be more comfortable, since taking the subway involves going back and forth between the station halls and the train platforms, as well as going through luggage security checks, which are inevitable. Moreover, traveling by taxi is one of the recommended modes during off-peak hours. Whether hailing a taxi by the roadside or ordering a taxi ride through the online platform, you can quickly board the vehicle and set off. Particularly if you want to visit some scenic spots in the suburbs of Shanghai, such as Zhujiajiao Water Town, whose entrance to the scenic area is about 15 minutes' walk from the nearest subway station, taking a taxi can send you directly to the destination.
The taxi fare in Shanghai is relatively reasonable. The cost for traveling between attractions within the city is approximately CNY 40 - 80 (USD 6 - 12), while the fare for going to the airport or more distant suburban attractions is about CNY 150 - 300 (USD 23 - 45). 
3. By BusThere are diverse buses in Shanghai, including City Bus, Sightseeing Bus, Tourist Bus, as well as Long-distance Bus.
City Bus: The city buses have extensive routes covering almost everywhere around Shanghai, serving as an alternative to the metro and perfectly making up for the inconvenience of some subway stations being a bit far from the entrance of certain tourist attractions. During off-peak hours, you may consider traveling by city bus, which helps you save money and also offer you convenience to admire the street views along the journey.
Sightseeing Bus: Shanghai boasts a lot of sightseeing buses, allowing you to visit the city’s landmark attractions in one go. What’s more, the buses are equipped with headphones that support multiple languages, making it easier for you to understand the history and fascinating stories behind different attractions. The most recommended sightseeing bus route is City Sightseeing Line 1, which connects the Bund, Lujiazui, Yu Garden, Nanjing Road, and People’s Square, among other core attractions. Shanghai Sightseeing Bus Shanghai Tourist Buses 
Tourist Bus: There are many tourist buses heading for scenic areas that are far away from the city center or located in some nearby cities. For instance, you can take the tourist bus from Shanghai South Railway Station directly to Shanghai Disneyland Park in 40 minutes at the cost of CNY 10, which is more time-saving and relaxing than taking the crowded metro. Top 8 Shopping Areas in Shanghai
Shanghai, famed as the “Shopping Paradise” and the “Oriental Paris”, offers an irresistible allure that makes shopping an essential and unmissable part of any visit. Be it the pursuit of high-end luxury labels, the discovery of traditional Chinese souvenirs, or the immersion in the vibrant atmosphere of local markets, this metropolis unfailingly delivers a shopping escapade that is both superlative and all-encompassing.
1. Nanjing Road - The Most Prosperous Shopping Street
Nanjing Road is one of the most bustling shopping streets in Shanghai, stretching over five kilometers in length and divided into two parts. The eastern part is dotted with specialty stores and diminutive shops that offer a wide array of clothing and electronic items. On the west side, you'll find upscale shopping malls and flagship stores of international luxury brands such as Cartier and Dior. Along this vibrant thoroughfare, numerous cafes and restaurants are conveniently situated, affording weary shoppers a welcome respite. Additionally, there are tram lines running from one end of the street to the other, providing an energy-saving way to go shopping.
More to see:  East Nanjing Road, East Nanjing Road Shopping Malls & Restaurants, West Nanjing Road Nanjing Road, Shanghai A shopping mall on Huaihai Road 
2. Huaihai Road - Luxury Goods Gathering Place
Huaihai Road, a quintessential high-end fashion shopping boulevard in Shanghai, is home to a sprawling array of over 400 stores. It serves as a magnet for a multitude of international luxury brands. Renowned names such as Gucci, Chanel, and Louis Vuitton have established their flagship emporiums here, presenting the latest and trendiest collections of clothing, bags, shoes, and other fashionable accouterments of the current season.
3. Yuyuan Bazaar - The Grand Bazaar of Traditional Features
Yuyuan Bazaar, being one of Shanghai's historical and cultural landmarks, exhibits a distinctively unique Chinese traditional style. It houses a diverse range of Chinese-style commodities and handicrafts, accompanied by numerous food stalls. Here, visitors can purchase souvenirs that are rich in Chinese characteristics, such as silk products, antiques, jade, and traditional handicrafts, thereby enabling them to immerse themselves in and experience the alluring charm of Chinese traditional culture.  Yuyuan Bazaar, Shanghai An exquisite store in Tianzifang 
4. Tianzifang - The Fusion of Art and Shopping
Tianzifang, nestled in the French Concession of Shanghai, is a charming district where many edifices preserve the architectural essence of the 1930s. Comprising a labyrinth of narrow and winding alleys, it houses a profusion of art studios, galleries, and specialty boutiques. Here, one can relish the sight of avant-garde paintings, sculptures, photographic masterpieces, and other forms of artistic expression, while also having the opportunity to acquire handicrafts, exquisite jewelry, T-shirts emblazoned with artistic motifs, and other unique commodities. Moreover, it serves as a haven for photography aficionados, as even a spontaneous click can yield a photograph replete with artistic charm.
5. Xintiandi - The Trendy Place Blending the Old and the New
Xintiandi, a remarkable blend of tradition and modernity, as well as an integration of the East and the West. The northern block preserves the time-honored Shikumen buildings, while the southern block infuses new urban vitality. Surrounding the area, prosperous edifices host a variety of establishments such as gourmet restaurants, cozy book bars, exotic cafes, and high-end shopping malls. The nightlife here is also very rich. There are many bars and entertainment venues, which are good places for you to relax and feel the vitality of modern urban Shanghai after shopping. Xintiandi, Shanghai Prcelains in the Yunzhou Curio City 
6. Yunzhou Curio City - The Treasure Hunting Spot for Antique Collections
The Yunzhou Curio City, a significant antique trading market in Shanghai, houses hundreds of stalls brimming with a diverse range of antique treasures. Within it, one can discover antique porcelain pieces hailing from various epochs and exhibiting an array of shapes. Vintage cameras are also present, bearing the photographic memories of bygone times, and old vinyl records that enable one to savor the charm of the music from years past.
7. AP Plaza – A Paradise for Budget Shoppers
The AP Plaza is renowned for its budget-friendly offerings. The stalls are densely populated with an extensive assortment of merchandise. Here, one can encounter “substitute” items of clothing in the styles of various prominent brands, sporting diverse designs that stay in tune with the latest fashion fads. Despite their lack of authenticity, the prices are highly accessible. If the genuineness of the products is not a concern for you and you place greater emphasis on cost-effectiveness and distinctive aesthetics, then exploring this market for a shopping spree will prove to be an engaging and enjoyable experience.
8. The South Bund Fabric Market - The Ideal Place for Custom-Made Clothing South Bund Fabric Market, Shanghai 
The South Bund Fabric Market stands as an optimal destination for bespoke clothing. It presents a rich selection of fabrics, such as silk, chiffon, leather, and others, which vary in both material and color. Be it an elaborate dress, a trendy suit, or a traditional Chinese cheongsam or gown, the proficient tailors here are capable of customizing it to your precise specifications. Bargaining is a common practice in this market. You can engage in price negotiation with the tailors and thereby obtain satisfactory custom-made clothing at a more economical price.

Yu Garden
 Yu Garden, aka Yuyuan Garden, Yu Yuan in Chinese, is a classical garden ranking among the must-see attractions in Shanghai. It dates back to the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) and was owned by a government officer named Pan Yunduan. Yu in Chinese means pleasing and satisfying, and this garden was specially built for Pan’s parents as a place for them to enjoy a tranquil and happy time in their old age. Pond and Cloister of Yu Garden
  Yuyuan Garden Pictures  Yuyuan Garden Video  Video of Yuyuan Tourist Mart  
Facts about Yu GardenLocation: No. 137, Anren Street, Huangpu District, very close to the Old City God Temple
Area: 20,000 square meters (about 5 acres)
Time Needed for a Visit: about 2 hours
History of Yu Garden Yuyuan Garden Map (Click to Enlarge) This garden was not constructed all at once since its inception in 1559. Instead, it was built in intermittent phases over nearly 20 years before the completion in 1590. After Pan Yunduan’s death, his family fell into decline, so the garden was poorly maintained and changed hands several times. 
In 1760, to prevent the further decline of this garden, local wealthy merchants and gentry pooled funds to purchase Yu Garden and donated it to the Old City God Temple  nearby. The restoration of the garden took over 20 years, involving the reconstruction of pavilions and the addition of rockeries, among other efforts. Since the Old City God Temple already had an “East Garden” at the time, Yu Garden was named the “West Garden” to complement it. Later, Yu Garden was severely damaged again in wars. In 1956, the Shanghai government initiated restoration efforts, renamed the Old City God Temple’s “East Garden” as “Inner Garden”, and incorporated it into Yu Garden. In 1961, the Yu Garden was then officially opened to the public.
What to See in Yu Garden?Although the scale of Yu Garden is not too large, it contains all elements that a classical Chinese garden should have—the pavilions, halls, rockeries, carvings, ponds and cloisters, all of which have unique characteristics. Here are some highlights in the garden that you would not want to miss.  Pavillion and Pond in Yu Garden Exquisite Carvings in Yu Garden  
Great RockeryUpon entering Yu Garden, you will encounter a field of rockery which is called the Great Rockery. With a height of 14 meters (about 50 feet), it’s the largest as well as the oldest one in the southern region of the Yangtze River. Standing at the small pavilion on the top of it, you can get a bird’s eye view of the whole garden.
Sansui HallSansui Hall features five bays, standing at a height of 9 meters. It’s the most commodious structure in the garden. This Hall was originally called Leshou by Pan, which means joy and longevity, and was used to entertain guests. Later in the Qing Dynasty (1636-1912), it was renovated and renamed as “Sansui”, symbolizing prosperous official career and the proper utilization of talents, as well as the people’s aspiration for bountiful harvests and favorable weather conditions. It served as a venue for official ceremonies, the dissemination of imperial edicts, and gatherings of local gentry. Elegant Furniture in Yu Garden  
Wanhua ChamberWanhua Chamber is a two-story delicate building surrounded by devious cloisters. Its architectural details all carry a profound cultural significance: the fence is engraved with patterns of Chinese legends’ magical weapons and the traceries of the windows at the four corners of the ground floor are carvings in plum, orchid, bamboo and chrysanthemum shapes, respectively, symbolizing the presence of flowers throughout four seasons. In front of the Chamber stand two old trees, one being the 21-meter-tall (about 70-foot) ginkgo tree said to have been planted by the owner of Yu Garden over 400 years ago, and the other being the southern magnolia tree with a history of more than 100 years. Pavilions of Yu Garden  
Dianchun HallDianchun Hall, built later in the Qing Dynasty, was a place where families gathered for feasts on festive occasions. If you look at the details of this area, you will find there are many sculptures with the meaning of warding off evil spirits. In front of the hall, there is a water-facing opera stage. To the west is the “Cloud-Piercing Dragon Wall” featuring a clay dragon head with a tiled dragon body. This unique type of design is highly recognizable since it’s rarely seen in gardens of southern region of the Yangtze River. Cloud-Piercing Dragon Wall  
Yuhua Hall“Yuhua” means the “magnificence of the jade”, so Yuhua Hall is also known as “Jade Magnificence Hall”. It is a graceful constructure with furnishings made of top-grade rosewood and was originally the study of Pan where he read books and met friends. Stepping inside, you can still see Pan’s precious items such as the Four Treasures of the Study——writing brush, ink stick, paper, and ink stone, and the purple sandalwood drawing table.
Exquisite Jade RockThe true treasure of Yu Garden is the Exquisite Jade Rock, one of the three most famous rockeries in south China. It’s 3.3 meters (about 10.8 feet) in height and has 72 holes. What is interesting about this rock is that if you burn a joss stick from its bottom, the smoke will magically float out from all the holes. Similarly, while you pour water into the rock from its top, the water will flow out from each hole, creating a spectacular sight to see. Yuhua Hall, located opposite the Exquisite Jade Rock, was specifically built for the purpose of appreciating this wonderful artifact. Exquisite Jade Rock  
Inner GardenThe Inner Garden is long and narrow, but it is a very exquisite "garden within a garden". When entering this area, the first thing that catches your eye is the Hall of Serenity. Sitting in the hall, you can calmly observe the numerous strange peaks and rocks on the opposite side. Next is the Pavilion of Watching Waves. As the name suggests, when you climb up this pavilion and look eastward, you can see the waves of the Huangpu River. The most special feature is the Ancient Opera Stage. Its top is formed by the intersection of 22 circles and 20 arcs, which enables the singing to produce a lingering sound effect. In addition, there is a mirror on the top of the stage, and around it are 28 golden birds spreading their wings, creating a magnificent and exquisite visual effect.
What to Do in Yu Garden Area?Apart from admiring those marvelous architectures, you have a lot of other interesting things to do around Yu Garden.
Stroll Around the Yuyuan BazaarYuyuan Bazaar, on the periphery of Yu Garden, is a lively marketplace where all kinds of traditional craftworks, souvenirs, and food stalls are displayed in abundance. What a fulfilled journey to stroll along this street after exploring the garden! As a friendly reminder, bargaining is necessary. The Commercial Street  
Appreciate the Night View on the Nine Bend BridgeThe zigzag Nine Bend Bridge is a part of Yu Garden, but outside the area that charges entrance fee. At night, colorful lights on both sid
